strengths: Elegant and theoretically grounded formulation mapping the post-training alignment of flow matching models to Adversarial Imitation Learning (AIL).

Provides two distinct, well-derived algorithmic variants: FAIL-PD (pathwise derivative utilizing a novel one-step denoising approximation) and FAIL-PG (policy gradient using flow policy optimization with a GRPO/PPO-style update).

Extensive and highly convincing empirical validation across continuous text-to-image (FLUX.1-dev), video generation (Wan2.1), and discrete autoregressive generation (Xomni), proving the versatility of the method.

Insightful analysis of optimization dynamics, demonstrating that FAIL-PD provides superior long-term stability while FAIL-PG excels in convergence speed, and showing that FAIL can act as an effective regularizer to mitigate reward hacking.
weaknesses: High computational cost and training complexity: FAIL-PG has substantial wall-clock overhead (Table 14), and adversarial training inherently introduces sensitivity to hyperparameters and discriminator design.

Strong dependency on SFT cold start: Without behavioral cloning initialization, direct adversarial alignment causes a noticeable drop in prompt-following performance (UniGen drops from 63.38 to 55.23).
Minor presentation issues: There is a broken cross-reference ('Figure ??') in Section G.1 on page 19 which refers to the convergence visualizations.

strengths: Elegant conceptual formulation that reframes generative model post-training as Adversarial Imitation Learning (AIL), effectively bridging the gap between supervised fine-tuning (Behavioral Cloning) and preference-based reinforcement learning.

Comprehensive algorithm design proposing both FAIL-PD (a white-box pathwise derivative method with a computationally efficient one-step denoising approximation) and FAIL-PG (a black-box policy gradient method), catering to different constraints and modalities.

Strong and rigorous empirical validation on a state-of-the-art flow matching model (FLUX.1-dev), showing notable improvements on established benchmarks (UniGen-Bench, DPG-Bench, HPSv3) utilizing a relatively small dataset of 13k single-sample demonstrations.

Demonstrated versatility across diverse settings: successful transfer to discrete token-based image generation (Xomni) and video generation (Wan2.1), alongside acting as a powerful regularizer to prevent reward-hacking in traditional reinforcement learning.
weaknesses: High computational overhead during training. Because the framework is on-policy, online generation (rollout) constitutes the vast majority of training time (~40 seconds per step as shown in Table 14). This makes training resource-intensive, requiring 32 NVIDIA H20 GPUs in the paper's setup, which limits its accessibility for resource-constrained environments.

The practical superiority of FAIL-PD over FAIL-PG is somewhat marginal given its added complexity. FAIL-PD requires white-box access to propagate gradients through the vector field, yet converges much slower (taking 800 steps to match FAIL-PG's 400-step performance) and ends up with very similar final metric improvements.

Minor editorial oversights and formatting errors, such as using the placeholder/internal name 'Nano Banana pro' for Gemini 3 Pro in the abstract, a broken reference ('Figure ??') in Appendix G.1, and several minor typos in the appendix (e.g., 'exxcessively', 'conection', 'betwwen').

strengths: Novel formulation of generative model post-training as Adversarial Imitation Learning (AIL), providing a unified framework that bridges Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Reinforcement Learning (RL).

Dual algorithm design: FAIL-PD (white-box pathwise derivative utilizing differentiable ODE steps) and FAIL-PG (black-box policy gradient using flow policy optimization) are theoretically grounded and cater to different practical settings (continuous vs. discrete/autoregressive).

Comprehensive and large-scale empirical evaluation on state-of-the-art architectures, including FLUX.1-dev, Wan2.1 (video), and Xomni (discrete text-to-image), demonstrating consistent and significant improvements over SFT and RL baselines.
The proposed method acts as an effective regularizer to mitigate 'reward hacking' when combined with static reward models, showing visible improvements in image quality and semantic adherence.
Well-written manuscript with rigorous analysis of training stability, discriminator choices, and extensive appendix containing detailed derivations and qualitative results.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty of applying adversarial training to diffusion/flow-matching models is somewhat incremental given existing works such as ADD (Adversarial Diffusion Distillation) and LADD, although the imitation learning framing is clean.

The one-step denoising approximation (Eq. 2) simplifies training but introduces estimation errors under non-linear vector fields, which could be discussed more deeply regarding its impact on complex prompts.

Presence of writing polish issues and typos: an unresolved LaTeX broken reference 'Figure ??' on page 19; typo in the abstract 'from Nano Banana pro' (likely a placeholder or codename for Gemini 3 Pro); and minor citation typos like 'OpneAI' instead of 'OpenAI' on page 11.

Adversarial training is historically sensitive to hyperparameters. Although multiple stabilization techniques (hybrid training, cold start) are utilized, the optimization complexity remains a practical bottleneck for wide adoption.

strengths: Provides a clean and well-motivated formulation of flow-matching post-training alignment as adversarial imitation learning (AIL), eliminating the need for expensive pairwise preference datasets.

Derives two distinct and practical algorithms: FAIL-PD (pathwise derivative) utilizing the differentiable nature of deterministic ODE solvers, and FAIL-PG (policy gradient) for discrete/black-box settings, detailing their convergence and stability trade-offs.
Demonstrates exceptional performance improvements over strong baselines (SFT, RLHF, Online DPO) on established benchmarks (UniGen-Bench, DPG-Bench, HPSv3) using the state-of-the-art FLUX.1-dev model.

Exhibits great generalization capability, extending the framework successfully to video generation (Wan2.1) and discrete image generation (Xomni), as well as serving as a robust regularizer to mitigate reward hacking in standard RL.
weaknesses: The single-step denoising approximation (Equation 2) in FAIL-PD is a critical component for computational efficiency, but its empirical effects on gradient accuracy are not extensively ablated (e.g., comparing multi-step backpropagation vs. single-step).

The computational overhead of training a massive generator (FLUX.1-dev) alongside a large multimodal discriminator (Qwen3-VL-2B) is not explicitly discussed or quantified in terms of VRAM, throughput, or wall-clock training time compared to simpler alternatives like SFT or DPO.

Adversarial training is notoriously unstable, and the paper notes sensitivity to hyperparameters as a limitation. A systematic ablation on key hyperparameters, such as the KL divergence coefficient (β) or generator-to-discriminator update ratios, is lacking.

strengths: Elegant formulation that frames the post-training alignment of flow matching models as an Adversarial Imitation Learning (AIL) problem, bridging Supervised Fine-Tuning (Behavioral Cloning) and Preference Optimization.

The derivation of two distinct algorithms, FAIL-PD (pathwise derivative) and FAIL-PG (policy gradient), makes the framework versatile and applicable to both continuous-time white-box dynamics and black-box discrete/autoregressive setups.

Impressive empirical performance on FLUX.1-dev utilizing only 13,000 single-sample expert demonstrations, outperforming strong baselines like Online DPO and standard SFT across multiple standard benchmarks (UniGen, DPG-Bench, HPDv3).
Excellent generalization across modalities, with successful application to discrete autoregressive text-to-image generation (Xomni) and video generation (Wan2.1).

The work demonstrates that FAIL can act as a powerful regularizer when combined with static reward models (e.g., HPSv3), preventing the standard reward hacking and oversaturation problems typical in Reinforcement Learning.
weaknesses: Adversarial training is known to be unstable, and FAIL-PG indeed suffers from sudden mode collapse after ~450 steps as shown in the training dynamics (Figure 2). This limits its long-horizon training usability compared to FAIL-PD.

The paper lacks a comprehensive breakdown of the computational overhead. Running large VLMs (like Qwen3-VL-2B) or FLUX backbones as discriminators during online training introduces significant computational and memory overhead. A quantitative analysis of training costs (GPU-hours, memory consumption) compared to SFT or DPO is missing.

The FAIL-PD method relies on a single-step denoising approximation (Equation 2) to bypass expensive backpropagation through the entire ODE solver path. A deeper analysis or ablation on how much this local linearity assumption affects the gradient direction compared to a multi-step backpropagation is not provided.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: post-training alignment of flow matching models without requiring costly pairwise human preference data, framing it as an adversarial imitation learning (AIL) problem.

The proposed framework is versatile, offering two distinct optimization strategies: a pathwise derivative estimator (FAIL-PD) for differentiable ODE settings and a policy gradient estimator (FAIL-PG) for black-box/discrete settings.

The authors evaluate their method on multiple generation modalities, including high-resolution text-to-image (using FLUX.1-dev), video generation (Wan2.1), and discrete autoregressive token generation (Xomni).
The experimental results demonstrate that combining FAIL-PD with direct reward optimization can serve as an effective regularizer to mitigate reward hacking.
weaknesses: Mathematical formulation of FAIL-PG (Section 2.2): The approximation of the pointwise log-probability as the negative Conditional Flow Matching (CFM) loss (\log \pi_\theta(x) \approx - L_{CFM}(\theta, x) + C) is theoretically problematic. For Continuous Normalizing Flows (CNFs), the log-likelihood is computed via the change-of-variables formula, which requires integrating the divergence of the vector field. Neglecting this divergence term means that the CFM loss difference does not accurately represent the log-likelihood ratio of a specific sample across different policies, making the foundation of FAIL-PG mathematically unsound.

Numerical stability of FAIL-PD (Section 2.1): In Equation 2, the single-step denoising approximation uses the denominator 1 - (t + \Delta t). As the random timestep t approaches 1 - \Delta t, this denominator goes to zero. Differentiating through this term to compute pathwise derivatives scales the gradient by a factor that diverges as t approaches 1 - \Delta t. The paper does not address this mathematical singularity or explain how numerical stability is maintained during backpropagation.

Unfair baseline comparison (Section 3.2 & Appendix C.2): The paper compares FAIL against an RLHF baseline where a reward model (RM) is trained offline on initial policy rollouts vs. expert data and then frozen. It is well-known that optimizing against a frozen RM leads to reward hacking. In contrast, the discriminator in FAIL is trained dynamically online alongside the generator. A fairer baseline would be online RL or online reinforcement learning with a dynamically updated reward/preference model, rather than comparing an online minimax game to an offline frozen reward optimization.

Limited novelty over existing adversarial diffusion methods: Training diffusion or flow matching models with discriminators using single-step denoising or pathwise gradients is highly related to existing adversarial diffusion distillation and alignment methods (e.g., ADD, DMD2, UFOGen). The conceptual framing of these methods as Adversarial Imitation Learning (AIL) or Deterministic Policy Gradient (DPG) does not sufficiently differentiate FAIL from these prior works.
